qs.q: Which register is employed to hold the instruction/data coming from an I/O device?
e: In the fetch-execute cycle (operand fetch), memory accesses use MAR (address) and MBR (data).
For I/O accesses the lecture uses the I/O counterparts: I/O AR holds the address of the I/O operand, and I/O BR (I/OBR) holds the data coming from the input device (I/O BR ← data from input device).
So the register that holds what arrives from an I/O device is I/OBR. I/OAR only holds the address, CS is a code segment register, and IMR is not part of the lecture's register set.

qs.q: In an asynchronous bus using the STROBE signal, the slave reads on the falling edge of STROBE.
qs.e: An asynchronous bus has no clock; it uses a handshaking protocol. STROBE is the master-to-slave signal and the slave reads on its falling edge. ACK is the slave-to-master signal and the master reads on its falling edge. Therefore the statement is True.

qs.q: USB 2.0 is capable of supporting a transfer rate of up to 480 Mbps.
qs.e: USB versions in the lecture: USB 1.0 supports 127 devices at 12 Mbps; USB 1.1 (full-speed) supports 12 Mbps; USB 2.0 (hi-speed) supports up to 480 Mbps and is backward compatible with USB 1.0 and 1.1 devices and cables. So the statement is True.

qs.q: In a 32-bit system (32 address lines), what is the maximum size of the addressable memory?
e: The lecture states that the width of the address bus corresponds to the maximum addressing capacity of the bus: 2^lines.
With 32 address lines the capacity is $2^{32}$ locations.
$2^{32} = 2^{2} \times 2^{30} = 4 \times 1\text{ G} = 4$ GB (byte-addressable memory).
256 MB = $2^{28}$, 8 GB = $2^{33}$ and 16 GB = $2^{34}$ need 28, 33 and 34 address lines respectively.

qs.q: What is the purpose of the clock in a CPU?

c.x: To handle input and output operations
To generate timing signals for the CPU's operations

qs.e: The lecture lists Clock among the control-bus signals: it is used to synchronize operations. A synchronous bus contains a clock that sends a sequence of 1s and 0s at timed intervals to synchronize bus operations, and the clock speed (MHz) determines how many instructions per second the processor can execute. Storing data is done by registers/memory, I/O is handled by I/O modules and memory access by the memory controller and control signals.

qs.q: What is the purpose of direct memory access (DMA) in a computer system?

c.x: To control access to shared memory
To transfer data between I/O devices and memory without CPU intervention
To execute instructions directly from memory

qs.e: In the lecture's bus master/slave table, DMA is the case where an I/O device acts as the bus master and memory is the slave. Likewise, the PCI bus lets a peripheral take control of the bus and transfer data directly to another peripheral/memory, which is called DMA. Therefore DMA moves data between I/O and memory without the CPU performing the transfer. The other options describe unrelated memory-management or execution functions.

qs.q: A memory unit is specified as 8K × 16 (words × bits per word). How many address lines and data lines are needed?
e: Address bus width gives the capacity 2^lines, and the data bus width equals the number of bits per word (one wire per bit).
Number of words: $8K = 2^{3} \times 2^{10} = 2^{13}$, so 13 address lines.
Bits per word = 16, so 16 data lines.
Answer: 13 address lines and 16 data lines.

qs.q: A memory unit is specified as 2G × 8 (words × bits per word). How many address lines and data lines are needed?
e: Address lines are found from the number of words (2^lines) and data lines from the word width.
Number of words: $2G = 2^{1} \times 2^{30} = 2^{31}$, so 31 address lines.
Bits per word = 8, so 8 data lines.
Answer: 31 address lines and 8 data lines.

qs.q: A memory unit is specified as 16M × 32 (words × bits per word). How many address lines and data lines are needed?
e: Use address lines = log2(number of words) and data lines = bits per word.
Number of words: $16M = 2^{4} \times 2^{20} = 2^{24}$, so 24 address lines.
Bits per word = 32, so 32 data lines.
Answer: 24 address lines and 32 data lines.

qs.q: A memory unit is specified as 256K × 64 (words × bits per word). How many address lines and data lines are needed?
e: Address lines = log2(number of words); data lines = bits per word.
Number of words: $256K = 2^{8} \times 2^{10} = 2^{18}$, so 18 address lines.
Bits per word = 64, so 64 data lines.
Answer: 18 address lines and 64 data lines.

qs.q: The two sub-cycles (phases) of the instruction cycle repeatedly performed by the IAS control unit are ______.
e: The lecture states that the IAS operates through the CU by performing an instruction cycle repetitively, consisting of two sub-cycles.
Fetch cycle: the opcode of the next instruction is loaded into IR and the address into MAR (from IBR or from memory through MBR).
Execute cycle: when the opcode is in IR, the control circuitry sends signals to move data or make the ALU perform the operation.
Hence the two phases are fetch and execution.

qs.q: In the ______ step, the execution of an instruction may require reading data from memory or an I/O module.
e: The fetch-execute cycle in the lecture includes Data Fetch (DF) / Operand Fetch (OF).
If the operand needs memory or I/O, the address is calculated, then MAR (or I/O AR) ← address of operand, a read signal is sent to memory or the input device, and MBR (or I/O BR) receives the data.
This is the Fetch data step. Fetch instruction brings the instruction itself, interpret (decode) only analyzes it, and process data is the execute step on already-available operands.

qs.q: Which control-bus signal indicates that data from the addressed location is to be placed on the bus?
e: Memory Read: data from the addressed location is placed on the bus.
Memory Write: data on the bus is written into the addressed location.
I/O Read: data from the addressed I/O port is placed on the bus.
I/O Write: data on the bus is output to the addressed I/O port.
The question mentions an address location (memory), and data going from it onto the bus, so the answer is Memory read.

qs.q: The address bus indicates which device has permission to use the bus and for what purpose (reading or writing from memory or an I/O device).
qs.e: The address bus only identifies where the information is being sent (the memory/I/O location), and its width gives the addressing capacity 2^lines. Bus request, bus grant (permission to use the bus) and the read/write indications (Memory Read/Write, I/O Read/Write) are signals of the control bus. So the statement is False.

qs.q: Each line in the data bus carries only one byte.
qs.e: Bus width is the number of wires in the data bus, and each individual wire carries one bit, not a byte. For example, a 32-bit data bus has 32 individual wires, each carrying one bit of data. So the statement is False.

qs.q: Which of the following buses is unidirectional?
e: The data bus is bi-directional: data flows in both directions between processor, memory and peripherals.
The address bus only carries addresses generated by the master (CPU) toward memory/I/O, so it is unidirectional (in the lecture's bus diagram the CPU only drives the address lines).
The control bus mixes signals in both directions (e.g. bus request from a module and bus grant from the CPU), and the system bus contains all three buses, so it is not unidirectional.

qs.q: In which type of bus is set-up faster than other transmissions, making it well suited for applications where messages are generated at irregular intervals (e.g. keyboard data entry)?
qs.e: From the lecture's advantages of the asynchronous bus: it is simple (no need to synchronize both sides), cheap (less hardware) and its set-up is faster than other transmissions, so it suits applications with messages generated at irregular intervals, such as data entry from the keyboard. Synchronous buses rely on a common clock (lower overhead, higher throughput), and semi-synchronous buses use the clock but allow wait states.

qs.q: Processor bandwidth determines how many instructions per second the processor can execute.
qs.e: For microprocessors the lecture defines Bandwidth as the number of bits processed in a single instruction, while the clock speed (in MHz) is what determines how many instructions per second the processor can execute. The statement attributes the clock-speed role to bandwidth, so it is False.

qs.q: An asynchronous bus is slightly more complex and expensive than a synchronous bus.
qs.e: In the lecture's comparison table, the asynchronous bus is simple and cheap (it needs less hardware), while the synchronous bus is the one that is slightly more complex with more expensive hardware (but has lower overhead and greater throughput). The statement reverses them, so it is False.

qs.q: The data bus is bi-directional, so it allows data flow in both directions along the wires.
qs.e: The data bus exchanges data between the processor, memory and peripherals and is bi-directional: data can be read from memory/I/O to the CPU and written from the CPU to memory/I/O over the same wires. The statement is True.

qs.q: The control bus carries the signals relating to the control and co-ordination of the various activities across the computer.
qs.e: The lecture defines the control bus as carrying signals from the CU relating to control and co-ordination of activities across the computer, such as Memory Read/Write, I/O Read/Write, Transfer ACK, Bus request/grant, Interrupt request/ACK, Clock and Reset. The statement is True.
